Services / Contractors

CONTRACTOR websites.

Endcap designs websites for general and specialty contractors, from tenant improvement builders to electrical, roofing, and concrete firms. Each site shows finished projects with the scope and location, lists the license and its classifications, and sends bid requests to the estimator with the plans attached.

Let’s talk What’s included

What’s included

What a contractor website includes

Every site is designed and built by Endcap, with the pages, forms, and integrations agreed in your proposal.

01

Projects with the scope written out

Each project page names the building type, the scope of work, the city, and the schedule, with photographs in order, so an owner can find work like theirs.

02

The license on every page

The license number appears in the footer of every page, and the classifications you hold are listed beside the services they cover, as California requires of contractor advertising.

03

Bid requests that reach the estimator

The request form asks for the address, scope, and timeline, accepts drawings or a link to them, and sends each request to the person who prices the work.

04

Service area pages

Pages for the cities and counties you work in describe the projects you have built there, so people searching nearby find you.

05

A statement of qualifications that matches

The website and the statement of qualifications you send with bids share one design, and the safety, insurance, and certification details are kept current on both.

06

Careers

Open field and office positions are listed with a short application, so hiring does not depend on a job board alone.

Details

Rules to get right in California

General information to plan the site around. It is not legal advice; your counsel owns the final wording of any compliance language.

From our work

For 5801 Lincoln in Buena Park, Endcap produced a property website, plans, and a seven-page leasing brochure that share one design. A contractor’s website and statement of qualifications are designed the same way, as one set.

See 5801 Lincoln
  • License number in advertisingEvery licensed contractor must include the license number in all construction contracts, in subcontracts and calls for bid, and in all forms of advertising, as prescribed by the registrar of contractors (Business and Professions Code section 7030.5). Source
  • Advertise only the classifications you holdIt is a misdemeanor to advertise construction work without a valid license in the classification advertised, and the statute counts any electronic transmission and directory listing as advertising. A licensed building or engineering contractor may advertise as a general contractor. The fine is $700 to $1,000, in addition to any other punishment (section 7027.1). Source
  • AccessibilityIn California, a violation of the federal ADA is also a violation of the Unruh Civil Rights Act (Civil Code section 51(f)), which sets damages of no less than $4,000 for each offense (section 52(a)). Project galleries and bid forms should work with a keyboard and a screen reader. Source
  • Permission to show a projectSome owners and general contractors restrict photographs or naming the project in their contracts. Confirm permission before a project page names the client or shows the interior.

FAQ

QUESTIONS,
answered.

Anything else? Ask us directly or email Noah at hello@endcap.design.

Where does the license number go on a contractor website?

California requires the license number in all forms of advertising, as prescribed by the registrar of contractors (Business and Professions Code section 7030.5). We put it in the footer of every page and beside the bid request form. The Contractors State License Board can confirm the current requirements for your license.

Can we show projects we worked on as a subcontractor?

Yes, with permission where the contract requires it. A project page can describe your scope on a larger job without suggesting you built the whole building.

Can the bid form accept drawings?

Yes. The form accepts plan files or a link to them, and sends the request to your estimator with the address, scope, and timeline.

Do you write the service area pages?

Yes. We write them from the projects and cities you actually work in, so each page describes real work instead of repeating the same text with a new city name.

How long does a contractor website take?

Most websites take two to four weeks once project photographs and descriptions are ready. The proposal confirms the schedule.

What does it cost?

Projects are quoted after a short conversation about the projects, pages, and forms involved. Scope, timing, and price are agreed in writing before work begins.
